notes.meaning: Lazarus was gravely ill in the village of Bethany, just outside Jerusalem. He lived there with his two sisters, Martha and Mary, and their home was a place where Jesus often stayed. The sisters were deeply concerned and looked to Jesus for help.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have suggested that the Lazarus in this account was connected to the poor man named Lazarus in Jesus' parable in Luke 16.

notes.meaning: John looks ahead to the well-known moment when Mary would pour costly perfume on Jesus and wipe His feet with her hair. She was famous among early believers for this humble act of love. John mentions it here so his readers clearly know which Mary he is talking about.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Western church tradition, seen in Augustine, sometimes identified Mary of Bethany with the unnamed repentant woman who anointed Jesus' feet in Luke 7.

notes.meaning: The sisters sent a messenger across the Jordan River to let Jesus know their brother was sick. They did not make demands or tell Him what to do, but simply brought their sorrow to the One who loved Lazarus. Their message shows deep humility and complete trust in His care.

Jesus assured His listeners that this sickness would not have permanent death as its final outcome. Instead, it was allowed so that God's power would be displayed and the Son of God would be honored through it. Even painful hardships can become occasions for God's glory to shine.

John reminds the reader that Jesus had a tender, personal love for Martha, Mary, and Lazarus. This shows that whatever Jesus did next came out of genuine affection, not neglect. Even when help seems delayed, believers can know that God's love for them has not changed.

After hearing the news, Jesus deliberately stayed where He was for two more days instead of rushing to Bethany. He waited so that Lazarus would be fully dead and buried before He arrived. This delay allowed room for a far greater miracle that would strengthen everyone's faith.

Once the two days were over, Jesus told His disciples that it was time to go back to Judea. He operated on God's timetable rather than human panic. Even though Judea was dangerous for Him, His love for His friends called Him back.

The disciples were alarmed because religious leaders in Judea had recently tried to stone Jesus to death. They could not understand why He would walk straight back into a place where people wanted to kill Him. Their fear for their Master made them hesitate to follow.

Jesus reminded them that daylight lasts twelve hours, giving plenty of time to travel safely without stumbling. He meant that God had set an exact time for His earthly work, and no harm could stop Him before that work was done. Following God's clear calling keeps a person safe from moral stumbling.

Traveling at night leads to stumbling because there is no sunlight to show the path. In a spiritual sense, anyone who walks outside of God's guidance and follows worldly fear is walking in darkness. Safety comes from following God's light, not from running away from duty.

Jesus told the disciples that their friend Lazarus had fallen asleep and that He was going to wake him up. In the Bible, sleep is a gentle word for death, reminding believers that the body's rest in the grave is not final. Jesus spoke of raising Lazarus from death as easily as waking a sleeping friend.

The disciples thought Jesus meant normal, restful sleep, which was usually a sign that a patient's illness was improving. They argued that if Lazarus was resting, he would get well on his own. In this way, they hoped to convince Jesus that there was no need to risk the journey to Judea.

The disciples took Jesus' words in the ordinary sense of physical rest. John explains that Jesus had actually been speaking about the death of Lazarus. Their confusion showed how slowly they caught on to spiritual language.

Seeing that they missed His meaning, Jesus spoke without figures of speech. He told them plainly and directly that Lazarus was dead. He knew this through His divine awareness, even though no human messenger had reported it.

Jesus said He was glad for their sake that He had not been there to prevent the death, because what they were about to see would build their faith. Raising a dead man after several days would provide far greater proof of His divine power than healing a sick man. Then He called them to go to Lazarus.

Thomas, whose name means the Twin, urged his fellow disciples to go along so they could die with Jesus. He was sure that returning to Judea would lead to their execution by hostile leaders. Though his words sound despairing, they reveal a brave and faithful loyalty to his Master.

When Jesus reached the outskirts of Bethany, He discovered that Lazarus had already lain in the tomb for four days. Jewish burial customarily took place on the very day of death. Four full days in the grave made it certain to everyone that Lazarus was completely and truly dead.

John explains that Bethany was less than two miles from the capital city of Jerusalem. Because it was so close, many people from the city could easily walk over to offer their condolences. This closeness also meant that whatever Jesus did would quickly be reported to the authorities.

A large crowd of Jewish friends and relatives came to sit with Martha and Mary to comfort them over the death of their brother. Jewish custom treated comforting mourners as an important religious duty lasting several days. God arranged this gathering so that many credible witnesses would see the coming miracle.

As soon as word reached Martha that Jesus was nearing the town, her active nature led her to go out and meet Him right away. Mary remained sitting in the house, silently keeping the traditional posture of deep grief. Martha took the lead to seek comfort from the Lord without delay.

Martha poured out her sorrow, telling Jesus that her brother would not have died if He had been present. Her words showed sincere faith in His power to heal the sick, but also the deep pain caused by His absence. Like many grieving people, she struggled to see how God could work once hope seemed lost.

Even in her grief, Martha confessed that God would give Jesus whatever He asked. She knew He had a unique bond with the Father and had not lost His authority. Her faith remained active even in the midst of her family's darkest hour.

differ.view: Some hold that Martha's words show she already believed Jesus had the power to raise Lazarus from the dead right then.
Others understand her words not as expecting Lazarus to be raised now, but as expressing lasting trust in Jesus despite not getting what she had hoped for.

notes.meaning: Jesus comforted Martha with the direct promise that her brother would rise again. He stated this simply, without specifying whether He meant immediately or at the final resurrection, which is the raising of all the dead at the end of time. His words were meant to test her faith and prepare her heart for what was coming.

Martha replied that she knew Lazarus would rise on the last day, when God raises the dead at the end of the world. Belief in the final resurrection was widely taught and accepted among faithful Jews of her time. Yet this distant truth did little to remove the immediate ache of losing her brother today.

Jesus told Martha that He Himself is the resurrection and the life. He is not merely a teacher pointing to a future event, but the living source and author of all life who holds total power over death. Anyone who trusts in Him will live forever, even if their physical body dies.

Jesus added that anyone who lives and trusts in Him will never experience true, eternal death, which is final separation from God. Physical death is only a temporary sleep for the believer, because the life Christ gives cannot be destroyed. Then He asked Martha directly whether she believed what He had just said.

Martha responded with a magnificent confession of faith. She stated that Jesus is the Christ, meaning God's promised King, and the Son of God who was sent into the world. Her confidence rested entirely on who Jesus was, even before she saw any miracle take place.

After making her confession, Martha went back home and quietly whispered to Mary that the Teacher was nearby and asking for her. Calling Jesus 'the Teacher' was the respectful title their household regularly used for Him. Martha spoke in secret so the gathered crowd of visitors would not cause a commotion.
